findings.title: Regex fallback silently drops # haute:preserve-start/end blocks, causing data loss on the next save
findings.description: fallback_parse builds the returned PipelineGraph without ever extracting preserved blocks. The healthy parser (parser.py:165-176) calls `_extract_preserved_blocks(source)` and passes `preserved_blocks=...` to PipelineGraph; the fallback omits this entirely. `PipelineGraph.preserved_blocks` defaults to `[]` (_types.py:652), so any code the user fenced with `# haute:preserve-start` / `# haute:preserve-end` is absent from the recovered graph. When the GUI later saves the (still syntactically-broken-on-disk) file, codegen reads `graph.preserved_blocks` (codegen.py:932/1243) and emits them via `_emit_preserved_blocks` (codegen.py:728-729); because the parser never populated them, the preserved code is permanently dropped from the regenerated file. `_extract_preserved_blocks` is pure line-scanning (no AST), so it works on broken source and could be called here. This is the same data-loss-on-save failure mode as the known submodel finding, but a distinct artifact (preserved blocks).
findings.evidence: fallback_parse return omits preserved_blocks=; PipelineGraph.preserved_blocks default_factory=list (_types.py:652); codegen.py:932 `all_preserved = ... graph.preserved_blocks`; codegen.py:728-729 emits them. _extract_preserved_blocks (_ast_helpers.py:520-548) is text-only and import-available in this module's _ast_helpers import group.

findings.title: Unreachable config-inferred-type branch and unused recovered_type
findings.description: Inside the `config_kwarg` recovery block, `loaded_config, recovered_type = recovered` is unpacked, then `if not block['explicit_node_type']: node_type = recovered_type`. `block['explicit_node_type']` is set in _find_function_blocks (line 563) to `DECORATOR_TO_NODE_TYPE[decorator_method]`, and `decorator_method` is filtered to be a key of that dict (line 522). Every value in DECORATOR_TO_NODE_TYPE is a non-empty NodeType StrEnum member (all truthy). Therefore `not block['explicit_node_type']` is always False, lines 690-691 never execute, and `recovered_type` is never used. node_type was already initialised to the same explicit_node_type at line 677, so the branch can never change it.

So line 690 guard is statically always False.
findings.est_reduction: ~4 lines + simplify unpack to `loaded_config, _ = recovered`

findings.title: A wrapped (multi-line) def signature aborts the ENTIRE fallback parse instead of recovering other nodes
findings.description:
_find_decorated_def matches the function header with `re.match(r'def\s+(\w+)\s*\(([^)]*)\)', line)` on a single physical line. A valid but line-wrapped signature (e.g. `def foo(
    a,
    b,
):`) has no closing `)` on the `def` line, so the match is None and the function raises ParseError. fallback_parse calls _find_function_blocks at line 670 without any try/except, so this ParseError propagates out of fallback_parse and aborts recovery of the WHOLE file — every node and edge is lost, not just the one node with the wrapped signature. Because the fallback only runs on files that already failed ast.parse, the realistic trigger is a hand-edited file whose syntax error is elsewhere (e.g. a typo in one body) while an unrelated, perfectly valid node happens to use a multi-line signature. The whole-graph abort defeats the module's stated 'best-effort graph the GUI can render alongside error markers' purpose. (Codegen always emits single-line signatures, so codegen-produced files are unaffected.)
findings.evidence: _find_decorated_def:491 `match = re.match(r"def\s+(\w+)\s*\(([^)]*)\)", line)`; lines 493-497 raise ParseError when match is None. fallback_parse:670 `blocks = _find_function_blocks(source)` is uncaught; _find_function_blocks:526 calls _find_decorated_def. `[^)]*` cannot span the newline of a wrapped signature.

findings.title: Trailing backslash inside a comment on the previous line is misread as a line continuation, skipping a valid top-level connect
findings.description: _has_backslash_continuation_before tests `previous_line.rstrip().endswith('\\')` on the raw text of the previous physical line. A backslash at the end of a comment (e.g. `# see foo \`) or inside a string is NOT a Python line continuation, but this check treats it as one. _is_top_level_statement_anchor returns False when this helper is True (line 181), so a genuine module-level `pipeline.connect(...)` on the following line would be classified as a non-top-level continuation and skipped by _iter_connect_anchor_matches, silently dropping that edge. The helper inspects raw line text rather than code positions (it does not strip comments/strings the way the rest of the module's scanners do), which is the root inconsistency.
findings.evidence: _has_backslash_continuation_before:152 builds previous_line from raw source and returns `.rstrip().endswith('\\')`; _is_top_level_statement_anchor:181 `if wrapper_depth < 0 or _has_backslash_continuation_before(...): return False`. Unlike _skip_string_literal-based scanners elsewhere, no comment/string awareness is applied to the previous line.

findings.title: Fallback path skips _validate_user_contract, so a drifted contract= annotation is not caught at parse time
findings.description: The healthy parser resolves config through _resolve_node_config, which calls _validate_user_contract to cross-check a `contract=` kwarg against the builder-derived contract and raises ContractMismatchError on disagreement (_config_builder.py:434). fallback_parse builds config directly via _build_node_config and merely re-attaches `config['contract'] = decorator_kwargs['contract']` (lines 740-741) with no validation. Contract validation is config-only (it does not require the file to be syntactically whole), so a wrong/drifted contract annotation in a broken file silently survives parse-time. The mismatch is only re-detected later at execution time, diverging from the project's fail-loud-at-parse philosophy that the healthy path implements.
findings.evidence: _resolve_node_config:434 `_validate_user_contract(node_type, config, user_contract, func_name)` raises ContractMismatchError (_config_builder.py:364-372). fallback_parse never calls _resolve_node_config or _validate_user_contract; it only does the unconditional re-attach at 740-741. Compare _config_builder.py:441-442 which attaches AFTER validation.

findings.title: getGitHistory drops limit=0 via truthiness check, silently using backend default
findings.description: getGitHistory builds the query string with `const params = limit ? `?limit=${limit}` : ""`. Because the guard is a truthiness check rather than `limit !== undefined`, an explicit `limit === 0` is treated the same as omitted: the `?limit=` param is dropped and the backend falls back to its default (git_history's `Query(20, ge=1, le=500)` -> 20). The intent of passing an explicit number is silently ignored for the value 0. This is the only endpoint in the in-scope range that decides param inclusion by truthiness of a numeric value. Impact is minimal in practice: the sole caller (GitPanel.tsx:71) passes 30, and the backend would reject 0 anyway (ge=1), so this changes *which* behavior occurs (default 20 vs a 422) rather than corrupting data. Reported for completeness; the idiomatic fix is `limit !== undefined ? `?limit=${limit}` : ""` (mirroring the `streamingChunkSize !== undefined` pattern used elsewhere in this file).
findings.evidence: client.ts:1163-1168 `export function getGitHistory(limit?: number, options?) { const params = limit ? `?limit=${limit}` : ""; return request(`/api/git/history${params}`, options)... }`. Backend src/haute/routes/git.py:202 `def git_history(limit: int = Query(20, ge=1, le=500))`. With limit=0: `0 ?` is falsy => params="" => backend uses 20. Contrast client.ts:511 which uses `streamingChunkSize !== undefined` to avoid exactly this falsy-zero pitfall.

findings.title: failExploreJob relabels a previous explore report from a DIFFERENT config with the failed job's configHash, causing the panel to show stale cross-config data as the current result
findings.description: On an explore failure, failExploreJob unconditionally preserves the previously cached report (`result: previous?.result ?? null`) but stamps the new entry with the FAILED job's identity (`configHash: job.configHash`, `source: job.source`, `structuralVersion: job.structuralVersion`). When the failure is for a config that differs from the previously successful one, the stored entry now claims an old report belongs to the new config. ExplorePreview's freshness check matches purely on configHash+source (currentCachedResult = cachedResult.configHash === configHash && cachedResult.source === activeSource), so it will surface the stale report (`report = currentCachedResult?.result`) as the result for the new config, with no staleness indicator (explore has no isStale gate, unlike solve/train via useStaleConfigEstimate). The fix is to preserve previous.result only when previous.configHash === job.configHash && previous.source === job.source, else null — matching the solve/train semantics where a failed run for a changed config does not present an old result as current.
findings.evidence: Trace: (1) explore succeeds for config A -> exploreResults[nodeId] = { result: reportA, configHash: A, source: srcA }. (2) user changes config to B, runs explore, it fails -> failExploreJob(nodeId, err, term) with job.configHash = B (job came from startExploreJob with hash B). (3) previous = s.exploreResults[nodeId] = the A entry. (4) nextCached = { result: reportA, configHash: B, source: srcB, structuralVersion: vB, error: err }. (5) In ExplorePreview.tsx:91-95 currentCachedResult matches because configHash===B && source===srcB, so report = reportA and ExploreOverviewPane/DataPreview render reportA's rows/columns as if they are config B's data. The existing test useNodeResultsStore.test.ts:461-480 ('failExploreJob ... without discarding the previous report') exercises exactly this cross-config sequence (h1 -> startExploreJob h2 -> failExploreJob) and asserts cached.result === report while the entry's configHash becomes h2 — it locks in the mislabeling and never asserts configHash, so the bug is currently codified as intended.

findings.title: structuralVersion is threaded through every explore job/result but never read by any consumer — its freshness signal is already fully subsumed by configHash
findings.description: startExploreJob accepts a structuralVersion arg and stores it on ActiveExploreJob; completeExploreJob and failExploreJob copy job.structuralVersion onto CachedExploreResult. No code path ever reads CachedExploreResult.structuralVersion or ActiveExploreJob.structuralVersion to gate freshness (verified by grep across frontend/src). Explore freshness is decided solely by configHash+source in ExplorePreview, and configHash is computed from buildExploreCacheIdentity, which already snapshots the full upstream topology (each upstream node's id/type/label/nodeType/data-affecting config plus the connecting edges). Any structural change that affects the explore result already changes configHash, so the stored structuralVersion conveys nothing the hash does not. It is write-only redundant state (unlike previews/columns, which genuinely compare structuralVersion against useGraphStore). Removing the field from CachedExploreResult/ActiveExploreJob and the startExploreJob signature (and the three call sites in ExplorePreview.tsx) simplifies the explore plumbing with no observable behavior change.
findings.evidence: buildExploreCacheIdentity (frontend/src/panels/explore/cacheIdentity.ts:41-80) returns { nodeId, nodes:[{id,type,label,nodeType,config}], edges:[{id,source,target}], submodels, preamble } over the upstream closure, and configHash = hashConfig({ graph: cacheIdentity, source }) (ExplorePreview.tsx:83-86). grep for '.structuralVersion' shows reads only in useDataInputColumns / usePipelineAPI (previews & columns) — none on explore job/result objects; ExplorePreview reads structuralVersion only to PASS into startExploreJob, never to compare against a cached explore entry.
findings.est_reduction: ~8-12 LOC (1 interface field x2, 1 param, 3 call-site args, 2 nextCached assignments)
findings.behavior_preservation: structuralVersion on explore entries is never read, and the freshness it would represent is already captured by configHash (buildExploreCacheIdentity hashes the full upstream node/edge/config topology). Deleting it leaves configHash-based freshness, LRU trimming, and all rendered output identical.

findings.title: PreviewNodeResponse redundantly re-declares six fields already inherited from NodeResult
findings.description: PreviewNodeResponse `extends NodeResult`, and NodeResult (types.ts:138-144) already declares `timings?`, `memory?`, `node_statuses?`, `node_columns?`, `node_available_columns?`, and `node_schema_warnings?` with the exact same types and optionality. findings.title: Unreachable `|| ...` fallbacks on tableStatuses lookups (one re-runs O(n) status)
findings.description: `tableStatuses = tables.map((candidate, idx) => ratingTableStatus(candidate, idx, tables))` (line 218) has exactly one entry per table. `safeIdx = Math.min(activeTab, tables.length - 1)` is always a valid in-range index because `normaliseRatingTables(config)` is guaranteed to return at least one table (it returns `[defaultRatingTable(0)]` when `config.tables` is empty/non-array). Therefore `tableStatuses[safeIdx]` (line 219) and `tableStatuses[idx]` (line 226, where `idx` comes from the same `tables.map`) can never be `undefined`. Both `|| { state: 'problem', issues: [] }` and `|| ratingTableStatus(candidate, idx, tables)` branches are dead. The line-226 fallback is also a latent inefficiency: were it ever reachable it would recompute a full O(n) `ratingTableStatus` (which itself scans all tables for duplicate output columns) for every visible row, turning the list render into O(n^2).

So `tableStatuses[safeIdx]` and `tableStatuses[idx]` are always defined; the `|| ...` arms are never evaluated.

findings.title: Editing any table silently drops a table's `onMissing` policy via the normalise→commit round-trip
findings.description: The editor reads tables with `normaliseRatingTables(config)` and writes them back with `commitTables`/`updateTable` (`onUpdate('tables', next)`), where `next` is always reconstructed by `normaliseRatingTable` (ratingTableUtils.ts:29-48). That reconstruction keeps only {name, factors, outputColumn, defaultValue, entries} and omits `onMissing`. The backend treats `onMissing: "neutral"` as a meaningful, supported per-table miss policy (_rating.py:403-414 `_normalise_on_missing`, :515 `table.get('onMissing')`, and it is set programmatically on optimiser tables in _builders.py:1620). So if a rating-step table carries `onMissing: "neutral"` in its config and the user edits ANY field of ANY table in this editor (factors, output column, default, a single entry — all funnel through `commitTables(tables.map(...))`), every table in the array is rewritten without `onMissing`, reverting it to the default "error" policy and changing runtime semantics (a previously-tolerated miss now raises RatingTableMissError). Confidence is low because the same field is also dropped by the codegen emitter for user-authored tables (_codegen_builders.py:740-748 omits onMissing), so the canonical generated-Python form may not surface it for hand-authored tables in the first place; the editor is nonetheless a second, user-triggered strip point and has no UI to view or preserve the field.

Backend reads it: `_rating.py:515 on_missing = _normalise_on_missing(table.get('onMissing'))`; default is "error" (_rating.py:405-409). `addTable` (line 332-333) likewise never sets it.

findings.title: Cache button enabled for emit-true tables with zero selected columns — build 'succeeds' but preview can never load
findings.description: The cache-disable gate keys only on `t.emit` (`hasEmitTrue = v2.tables.some((t) => t.emit)`), but the backend's single source of truth for 'this table contributes a data port' is `table_is_emitting` = `emit AND at least one selected column` (`src/haute/_json_shred.py:155-176`). findings.title: Cache status display goes stale after an in-memory schema edit because resourceKey omits the volatile schema
findings.description: `JsonCacheButton` builds `resourceKey = dataPath + '::' + (configPath ?? '')` and passes it to `CacheFetchButton`, whose status `useEffect` re-runs ONLY when `resourceKey` changes (deps `[resourceKey]`, with an explicit exhaustive-deps disable that excludes the `getStatus` callback). The status check sends `volatile_schema` to `getJsonCacheStatusForSchema`, and the backend validates cache freshness against that schema's fingerprint. The button keeps showing 'Refresh Cache' plus the previous schema's row/col/size stats — implying a valid cache exists for the schema the user is now looking at — when the cache is actually stale for the edited schema (the 'Not cached yet' hint likewise won't reappear). This contradicts the stated working-principle-4 intent ('the build uses what the user is looking at') for the status surface. The build itself is unaffected (doFetch captures the live volatileSchema at click time); only the cached/not-cached badge and stats are stale until the user clicks or deletes.
findings.evidence: Line 98 `resourceKey={dataPath + "::" + (configPath ?? "")}` — no schema component. `CacheFetchButton.tsx:108-128` status effect deps `[resourceKey]` with `// eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps -- stable callback props`; the inline `getStatus` (ApiInputEditor lines 99-107) forwards `volatile_schema: volatileSchema` but a new closure identity does not re-run the effect. Backend status freshness is schema-fingerprint-dependent (status route calls into `is_per_port_cache_valid`, which keys on the v2 fingerprint).

findings.title: Downstream preview cascade mixes submodel edges with parent-graph nodes, so the cascade is silently dead when a node inside an opened submodel changes columns
findings.description: Inside fetchPreviewImmediate the cascade builds its adjacency from graphRef.current.edges but resolves its node set from resolveGraphFromRefs(...).nodes. When a submodel is drilled in, graphRef.current holds the SUBMODEL canvas (nodes+edges) while parentGraphRef.current is set, so resolveGraphFromRefs returns the PARENT graph's nodes. propagate therefore walks submodel edge IDs to compute reachableNodeIds, but drainReadyQueue looks those submodel child IDs up in cascadeNodes (= parent nodes) via cascadeNodes.find(n => n.id === nodeId). The lookup misses every time, so each downstream child hits the `if (!dsNode || !canPreviewNode(dsNode)) { settleNode(nodeId, false); continue }` branch and the cascade no-ops: downstream nodes inside a submodel never get re-previewed (their _columns / requestedPreviewColumns are not refreshed) after an upstream column change. At the top level parentGraphRef.current is null so resolveGraphFromRefs returns graphRef.current.edges/nodes and the two sources coincide — the defect is submodel-specific.
findings.evidence: Line 318 `const graph = resolveGraphFromRefs(graphRef, parentGraphRef, submodelsRef, preambleRef)` then line 319 `let cascadeNodes = graph.nodes`; resolveGraphFromRefs (buildGraph.ts:31-33) returns parentGraphRef.current.nodes/edges when parentGraphRef.current != null. propagate line 332 `const { edges } = graphRef.current` builds childrenBySource from the SUBMODEL edges; BFS at 346-353 yields submodel node IDs in reachableNodeIds. drainReadyQueue line 439 `const dsNode = cascadeNodes.find((n) => n.id === nodeId)` searches PARENT nodes → undefined → line 440-442 `if (!dsNode || !canPreviewNode(dsNode)) { settleNode(nodeId, false); continue }`. useSubmodelNavigation.handleDrillIntoSubmodel sets parentGraphRef.current to the parent while setNodesRaw/setEdgesRaw load the submodel into graphRef; useEdgeHandlers.onNodeClick (useEdgeHandlers.ts:351) calls fetchPreview unconditionally for nodes inside the submodel, so the path is reachable.

findings.title: Sync-banner close button renders mojibake "â€¢" instead of an ✕ icon (double-encoded character on disk)
findings.description: The dismiss button for the WebSocket sync-error banner has its label corrupted on disk. The on-disk bytes are `C3 A2 C5 93 E2 80 A2`, which is the UTF-8 encoding of three code points U+00E2 (â) U+0153 (œ) U+2022 (•) — i.e. the literal string "â€¢". This is a classic double-encoding of the intended close glyph U+2715 (✕, MULTIPLICATION X, correct UTF-8 `E2 9C 95`): the original `E2 9C 95` was decoded as Windows-1252 (E2→â, 9C→œ, 95→•) and re-saved as UTF-8. The button therefore displays the garbage string "â€¢" to the user rather than a close icon, in a banner that appears precisely when sync has failed (a stressful, visible moment). The directly-above sessionExpired banner uses a text "Reload" button and is unaffected, so only this control is broken — meaning the regression is easy to miss in review since the surrounding chrome looks fine.
findings.evidence: PowerShell byte dump of the JSX text node between `opacity-100">` and `</button>` on line 537 returns raw hex `C3 A2 C5 93 E2 80 A2`; UTF-8 decode = U+00E2 U+0153 U+2022. A full-file scan found this is the ONLY mojibake occurrence outside of code comments (NON_COMMENT_COUNT=1). `text.Contains(U+2715)` is False, confirming the intended ✕ glyph is absent. Contrast lines 332/337/357 which contain a correct em-dash (U+2014), proving the file mixes good and corrupted multibyte sequences.

findings.title: Active-node id and preview-gating logic duplicated three times instead of reusing activePanelNodeId / previewForActiveNode

findings.title: closePanel clears previewData but does not cancelPreview, leaving an in-flight backend request running and previewBusy stuck true after a full panel close
findings.description: closePanel() fully tears down the selection (setSelectedNode(null), lastSelectedNodeRef=null, setLastSelectedId(null), setPreviewDataRef.current(null)) but never calls cancelPreview(). If a preview fetch is in flight when the user closes the panel via onPaneClick (line 561 → closePanel), the request's seq is not invalidated and `requestStillCurrent()` stays true, so fetchPreviewImmediate's `.then` still runs setPreviewData(preview) (usePipelineAPI.ts:529) and setPreviewBusy(false) only fires when the network round-trip eventually settles. Because the panel is closed, activePanelNodeId is null and previewForActiveNode gates the repainted data out of view, so there is no visual corruption — but the backend preview keeps executing to completion (wasted compute, and any downstream cascade in propagate() keeps writing _columns into nodes via setNodesRaw at 463/539), and previewBusy remains true in the meantime. This is asymmetric with handleDeleteNode/handleSwapEdgeJoinInputs which deliberately call cancelPreview(), and with the keyboard-shortcut closePanel path. Confidence is low because no user-visible artifact results and the request aborts naturally once it finishes; flagged as a resource/robustness gap, not a display defect.

findings.title: Position-only dirty derivation's never-saved branch ignores edges/preamble (latent divergence from computeDirty)
findings.description: For the lastSavedSnapshot===null case, computeDirty returns `persistedFingerprint !== EMPTY_SNAPSHOT` (dirty if ANY of nodes/edges/preamble is non-empty), but the position-only sibling computeDirtyForPositionOnlyNodes returns `nodes.length > 0` only. On a never-saved workspace with zero nodes but non-empty edges or a non-empty preamble, these two disagree: computeDirty says dirty, computeDirtyForPositionOnlyNodes says clean. The two functions are meant to be drop-in equivalents for the position-only fast path. The divergence is currently UNREACHABLE because hasOnlyNodePositionChanges() (the only gate to this branch) returns false whenever both node arrays are empty (its per-index loop never runs, so positionChanged stays false), so setNodesRaw never reaches the position-only branch with nodes.length===0. It is therefore a dormant correctness inconsistency rather than an active bug, but it is a real trap for any future caller/refactor that reuses computeDirtyForPositionOnlyNodes or changes the gating predicate.
findings.evidence: computeDirty null-branch (line 360): `selectIsDirty({lastSavedSnapshot:null}, persistedFingerprint)` => `persistedFingerprint !== EMPTY_SNAPSHOT` where EMPTY_SNAPSHOT = serialize({nodes:[],edges:[],preamble:''}). computeDirtyForPositionOnlyNodes null-branch (line 385): `return nodes.length > 0` — only inspects nodes, never edges or preamble. selectIsDirty/EMPTY_SNAPSHOT defined in utils/graphSnapshot.ts:121,133-141. Unreachability: hasOnlyNodePositionChanges (228-253) returns `positionChanged` initialized false; for empty arrays the loop body is skipped so it returns false, so setNodesRaw (530) never enters the position-only branch when nodes is empty.

findings.title: Three change-classification helpers duplicate the same key-diff skeleton
findings.description: The three setNodesRaw/setEdgesRaw change classifiers share one verbatim skeleton: length guard -> per-index loop -> `previous === node` bail -> id-equality bail -> build `new Set([...Object.keys(previous), ...Object.keys(node)])` -> for each key, if it is a managed UI field record a `changed` flag via !Object.is(...), else require Object.is(prevValue,nextValue) and bail false otherwise -> finally return `changed`. They diverge only in which fields are 'tracked' vs 'bail': hasOnlyNodeUiFieldChanges treats position as an extra bail and data-ref as a bail; hasOnlyNodePositionChanges treats position as the tracked delta and UI fields as ignorable; hasOnlyEdgeUiFieldChanges drops position/data entirely. This is incidental duplication (~85 LOC) distinct from the already-known SIMP-02 (which targets the mutators' fingerprint/version bookkeeping, not these classifiers). Note this is a marginal cleanup: the per-helper divergence in tracked-vs-bail field roles means a unified helper would need a small config object, so the readability win is modest.
findings.evidence: hasOnlyNodeUiFieldChanges (196-226), hasOnlyNodePositionChanges (228-253) and hasOnlyEdgeUiFieldChanges (255-281) all contain the identical `const keys = new Set([...Object.keys(previous), ...Object.keys(node/edge)]); for (const key of keys) {... if (UI_FIELDS.has(key)) { if(!Object.is(prev[key],next[key])) changed=true; continue } if (!Object.is(prev[key],next[key])) return false }` block; the node variants additionally early-bail on `previous.data !== node.data` and `!positionsEqual(...)`. REACT_FLOW_NODE_UI_FIELDS (178-185) / REACT_FLOW_EDGE_UI_FIELDS (187) parameterize the only set difference.
findings.est_reduction: ~25-35 LOC if unified behind a single classifyFieldChanges(prev,next,{uiFields,extraBail,tracked}) helper
findings.behavior_preservation: A shared classifier driven by the per-call field-role config produces identical boolean results: same length/identity/id guards, same Object.is comparisons, same UI-vs-structural partition; only the extraction site moves. No observable change to setNodesRaw/setEdgesRaw outputs.

findings.title: window.open(..., "_blank") omits noopener — reverse tabnabbing
findings.description: handleSubmit opens the compare/PR URL with window.open(result.compare_url, "_blank") but does not pass "noopener,noreferrer". findings.title: Conditional-mode a11y "sentinel" IIFE renders a no-op element invisible to every user and unverified by any test
findings.description: In the conditional render path, an 18-line IIFE conditionally emits a <span className="result-value accent" data-accent ... aria-hidden="true" style={{position:'absolute',width:1,height:1,overflow:'hidden',clip:'rect(0,0,0,0)'}} />. Hence nothing relies on the sentinel's presence.

Deleting the IIFE leaves the rendered/queryable DOM unchanged for every covered case.

findings.title: Conditional branch matching indexes substituted-text branches by the expression-text branch index, assuming the two independent parses are positionally aligned
findings.description: `branches = parseBranches(expression.expression_text)` and `subBranches = parseBranches(calculation.substituted_text)` are parsed independently, then `isBranchMatched(idx)` reads `subBranches[idx]` using an index derived from iterating `branches` (line 481 `branches.map((branch, idx) => ...)`, line 472 `branches.some((b,i)=>...isBranchMatched(i))`). This is only correct if both strings parse into the same number of branches in the same order. They can diverge: (a) any of the known parseBranches mis-splits (a then/otherwise value containing the word 'when'/'otherwise') affects expression_text and substituted_text differently because their tokens differ, shifting the index mapping; (b) the backend's substituted_text can legitimately have a different branch shape (e.g. a pre-resolved or collapsed branch) than the raw expression_text. When they misalign, `subBranches[idx]` is the wrong branch, so `isBranchMatched` consults the wrong substituted result and the highlighted branch is wrong. This only bites when the backend does NOT supply taken_branch_index (line 461-463 backendTakenBranchIndex===null), i.e. the legacy fallback path; when taken_branch_index is present the index is used directly (line 482-486) and isBranchMatched is bypassed.
findings.evidence: Line 459 `const subBranches = parseBranches(calculation.substituted_text)`; line 470-473 `function isBranchMatched(idx){ const sub = subBranches[idx]; if(!sub?.result) return false; return sub.result.includes(resultStr) }`; line 475-477 `branches.some((b,i)=>!b.isOtherwise && isBranchMatched(i))`; line 481-486 maps over `branches` and, when backendTakenBranchIndex===null, calls `isBranchMatched(idx)` with the branches-index. No code aligns subBranches to branches by condition/position before indexing.

findings.title: parseBranches silently drops all text preceding an `otherwise` clause when no when/then pair is present
findings.description: After the when/then loop, parseBranches runs `text.slice(lastIndex).match(/otherwise\s+(.+)/i)` and, on a match, pushes a single otherwise branch. If the text contains `otherwise` but ZERO well-formed `when ... then ...` pairs, the loop makes no iterations (lastIndex stays 0), the otherwise-match captures only the text AFTER `otherwise`, and a branch is pushed — making branches.length === 1, which suppresses the `branches.length === 0` fallback that would otherwise have preserved the full text. The leading text before `otherwise` is therefore silently discarded. This is a distinct edge from the documented 'then-value contains when' mis-split: it is the no-when/then-at-all case. In practice conditionals always begin with `when`, so reachability is low, but the function is a general string parser and the discard is silent (no loud failure), violating the repo's 'fail loudly' preference.
findings.evidence: Line 80-87 while-loop produces 0 matches for input like "foo otherwise bar" (no `then`); line 89 `text.slice(0).match(/otherwise\s+(.+)/i)` captures "bar"; line 90-95 pushes {result:"bar", isOtherwise:true}; line 97-99 `if (branches.length === 0)` is now false so the raw-text fallback is skipped — "foo" is lost. Compare the clean path where text starts with `when`: the loop consumes the when/then, lastIndex lands at the ` otherwise`, and the prefix is preserved as branches.

findings.description: The local CalculationHeroProps.calculation interface declares `taken_branch?: string | null` (line 41), but the component only ever consumes `taken_branch_index` (line 460). `taken_branch` is read nowhere in CalculationHero.tsx. It mirrors the wider trace wire type (types/trace.ts), but on THIS component's prop surface it is dead: it can be removed from the local interface without affecting behaviour, narrowing the component's declared contract to what it actually uses. Low value; flagged for completeness.
findings.evidence: Grep for `taken_branch\b` in frontend/src shows it consumed only in types/guards.ts and types/trace.ts (parsing) and asserted in guard/TracePanel tests; within CalculationHero.tsx the only branch-index read is line 460 `calculation.taken_branch_index ?? takenBranchIndex`. No reference to `calculation.taken_branch` exists in the component.

findings.title: "Unmatched rows" counter can go negative because match counts are summed across independently-counted (possibly overlapping) rules
findings.description: The per-rule match counts are computed by counting, for EACH rule, every preview row that satisfies that rule independently (lines 142-168). `matchedRows` is then `matchCounts.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0)` and `unmatchedCount = totalRows - matchedRows` (lines 172-173), with no clamping. When two or more continuous rules overlap, a single row is counted once per matching rule, so `matchedRows` can exceed `totalRows`, making `unmatchedCount` negative. The Default counter at line 554 then renders e.g. "-2 of 100 rows". Overlapping continuous rules are an explicitly supported and merely warned-about state (see warnings block lines 193-198 and detectOverlaps). The backend never double-counts: src/haute/_rating.py _apply_banding builds a when/then chain (first-match-wins, lines 119-133), so a row is assigned by exactly one rule. The preview model (count-each-rule) therefore diverges from real assignment semantics and produces an impossible negative unmatched figure.
findings.evidence: matchCounts: rules.map(r => previewRows.filter(row => matchesContinuousRule(Number(row[column]), r)).length) counts each rule independently. matchedRows=sum(matchCounts); unmatchedCount=totalRows-matchedRows (lines 172-173). With rules [<=15 'A'] and [>=10 <=20 'B'] a row at 12 is counted by both, so two rules over 1 row => matchedRows=2 for 1 row; with totalRows=1, unmatchedCount=-1. Rendered verbatim at line 554: `{unmatchedCount} of {totalRows} rows`. Backend _rating.py assigns first-match-only, so the true unmatched is >=0.

findings.title: Breakpoint per-row "Matches" column is misaligned because match counts are derived from sorted/filtered rules but indexed by raw row order
findings.description: For breakpoints mode, matchCounts is built as `breakpointsToRules(bpRules, rightClosed).map(cont => count rows matching cont)` (lines 149-159). `breakpointsToRules` (bandingUtils.ts) FILTERS OUT rows with blank/non-numeric boundaries and SORTS the remaining boundaries ascending, and may APPEND an extra open-ended rule for a blank-boundary row. The resulting array length and order therefore do NOT correspond 1:1 to `factor.rules` (the raw breakpoint rows). However that same `matchCounts` array is passed to BreakpointGrid (line 488), which renders `matchCounts[i]` indexed by the raw breakpoint-row index `i` (BreakpointGrid.tsx lines 250-255, breakpoints.map((bp,i)=>...) with no sort). Whenever boundaries are entered out of order (a common transient state, also flagged by the order warning), or a blank/invalid boundary sits before a numeric one, each row's displayed Matches count belongs to a different band.
findings.evidence: Rows [{boundary:'65'},{boundary:'25'}]: breakpointsToRules sorts to [25,65] => contRules order [<=25, (25,65]]. matchCounts=[count(<=25), count((25,65])]. BreakpointGrid row0 (boundary 65) shows matchCounts[0]=count(<=25); row1 (boundary 25) shows matchCounts[1]=count((25,65]) — both wrong. Also rows [{25},{'',senior},{65}]: bounded sorts to [25,65], blank skipped+appended last => row1 (blank) shows matchCounts[1]=count((25,65]) instead of the open-ended count. No realignment exists between the editor's sorted contRules and the grid's raw-order rendering.

findings.title: Match counts include rules with an empty assignment that the backend silently drops
findings.description: Match counting for categorical (lines 142-147) and continuous/breakpoints (lines 152-168) only inspects the matching predicate (value equality / interval membership) and ignores whether the rule has a non-empty `assignment`. The backend (_rating.py _apply_banding) explicitly skips categorical rules with empty assignment (lines 88-92, `replace_strict` remap only includes non-empty assignments) and skips continuous rules with empty assignment (lines 124-126, `if not assignment: continue`). A rule that has a value/interval but a blank label thus contributes to the preview's matched count even though those rows actually fall through to the Default at runtime. This makes the preview over-report matches and under-report the unmatched figure for a partially-filled rule.
findings.evidence: Frontend categorical: previewRows.filter(row => String(row[column] ?? '') === cat.value).length — no check on cat.assignment. Frontend continuous: matchesContinuousRule(val, cont) — bandingUtils only parses ops/values, ignores assignment. Backend _rating.py: categorical builds remap only when assignment is non-empty (line 91); continuous chain does `if not assignment: continue` (line 126). So {value:'London', assignment:''} matches 0 rows server-side but is counted in the preview.

findings.title: removeFactor adjusts the active tab using safeIdx instead of the removed index, so deleting a tab before the active one silently moves the selection
findings.description: removeFactor filters out `idx` then only re-clamps the active index with `if (safeIdx >= next.length) setActiveIdx(next.length - 1)` (lines 113-114). It never accounts for removing a factor positioned BEFORE the currently-active one. When `idx < safeIdx` and `safeIdx` is still < next.length, no adjustment runs, so `activeIdx` keeps its old numeric value while every factor after the removed one shifted down by one — the highlighted/edited factor silently becomes a different column.
findings.evidence: factors [A,B,C,D], active index 2 (C). User clicks remove on tab A (idx 0). next=[B,C,D] (length 3). safeIdx=2 which is < 3, so the guard does not fire and activeIdx stays 2 => now resolves to D, not the C the user was editing. The active selection jumps to the wrong factor. Correct handling would decrement activeIdx when removing an index <= the active one.

findings.title: Histogram never draws boundary lines in continuous mode
findings.description: The histogram is rendered for both continuous and breakpoints modes (condition at line 209 allows banding==='continuous' || banding==='breakpoints'). But the boundaries array is only populated for breakpoints: the loop at lines 220-226 pushes `Number(bp.boundary)` solely inside `if (factor.banding === 'breakpoints')`. For continuous rules (which carry explicit cut points in val1/val2), no boundaries are ever extracted, so BandingHistogram receives boundaries=[] and renders the value distribution with no cut markers. BandingHistogram fully supports drawing boundary lines (BandingHistogram.tsx lines 88-104), so the continuous histogram is silently missing the visual cues that make it useful, an inconsistency with the breakpoints rendering.
findings.evidence: histogramData boundaries loop: `for (const r of (factor.rules||[])) { if (factor.banding==='breakpoints') { ...push Number(bp.boundary) } }` (lines 220-226). No branch reads ContinuousRule.val1/val2. Yet the gating condition at line 209 includes continuous, so a continuous factor with rules and previewRows shows bars but zero boundary lines.

findings.title: Type toggle has no selected/focusable option when factor.banding is 'continuous'
findings.description: The Type ToggleButtonGroup only offers options 'breakpoints' and 'categorical' (lines 354-357), but a factor's banding can legitimately be 'continuous' (the default from normaliseBandingFactors, from addFactor/duplicateFactor, and from older/pasted configs). When such a configured factor is shown, `value={factor.banding}` ('continuous') matches neither option, so in ToggleButtonGroup every button has aria-checked=false and tabIndex=-1 (ToggleButtonGroup.tsx lines 49-56). The radiogroup then has no keyboard-focusable member, and the user sees a toggle with nothing selected even though the factor is in a real mode. Switching away is possible by click, but the control misrepresents and is not Tab-reachable in that state.
findings.evidence: options=[{key:'breakpoints'},{key:'categorical'}] (lines 355-356). ToggleButtonGroup computes active=value===opt.key and sets tabIndex={active?0:-1}; with value='continuous' both actives are false => all tabIndex=-1, none aria-checked. addFactor creates banding:'continuous' (line 91) and duplicateFactor copies src.banding; a duplicated/added factor that later gets a column set reaches shouldShowTypeToggle while still 'continuous'.

findings.title: Paired key edits/removals normalize leftOn and rightOn independently, persisting unequal-length arrays the backend rejects
findings.description: In paired-key mode, both updatePairedKey (lines 113-117) and removePairedKey (lines 127-133) call normalizeKeyRows() separately on the left array and the right array. normalizeKeyRows trims TRAILING empty strings only. When a user clears the last cell on just one side (or removes a row that leaves a trailing blank on only one side), the two arrays are trimmed to different lengths and written to config that way. This violates the Polars left_on/right_on equal-length contract: the backend (src/haute/_edge_join.py:182-184) raises ConfigError('edgeJoin leftOn and rightOn must contain the same number of keys.') and the frontend analyzer (edgeJoinValidation.ts:147-149) emits 'leftOn and rightOn must contain the same number of keys.' So a single ordinary cell edit produces a malformed, runtime-rejectable config plus a spurious diagnostic, instead of keeping the pair aligned.
findings.evidence: Start paired config leftOn=['a','b'], rightOn=['c','d'] (2 rows). User clears Join key 2 (right side, index 1) to ''. updatePairedKey('right',1,''): nextLeft = replaceAt(['a','b'],1,pairedRows[1].left='b') = ['a','b']; nextRight = replaceAt(['c','d'],1,'') = ['c','']. Then onUpdate({on:[], leftOn:normalizeKeyRows(['a','b'])=['a','b'], rightOn:normalizeKeyRows(['c',''])=['c']}). Result leftOn length 2 != rightOn length 1 -> ConfigError at runtime. The fix is to keep paired arrays aligned (pad to the max length, or only drop a row when both sides are blank) rather than trimming each side independently.

findings.title: Component-level nodeMap duplicates the map already built inside analyzeEdgeJoinNode and is used only for two role-edge labels
findings.description: EdgeJoinEditor builds `new Map(allNodes.map(...))` on every render (line 61) solely to resolve the source label of baseRoleEdge and joinRoleEdge via nodeLabel() in the two RoleDisplay instances. analyzeEdgeJoinNode already constructs an identical nodeMap internally (edgeJoinValidation.ts:92) and already returns baseRoleEdge/joinRoleEdge plus a connectedInputs list that carries each source's resolved label. So the full node map is built twice per render (O(N) over all graph nodes) just to look up two labels that the analysis pass could surface directly. RoleDisplay is not memoized, so passing the fresh Map costs nothing extra, but the second full map build and the local nodeLabel helper (lines 518-520) are redundant with the analyzer.
findings.evidence: Line 61 `const nodeMap = new Map(allNodes.map((node) => [node.id, node]))`; line 62 calls analyzeEdgeJoinNode which at edgeJoinValidation.ts:92 builds the same map. nodeMap is consumed only at lines 184/191 (RoleDisplay nodeMap prop) -> RoleDisplay line 383 `nodeLabel(roleEdge.source, nodeMap)`. The analysis return already exposes baseRoleEdge/joinRoleEdge and connectedInputs[].label, which could provide the two needed labels without a second map over every node.
findings.est_reduction: ~3-6 lines (drop local nodeMap + nodeLabel helper; pass precomputed labels from analysis)

findings.title: handleCellClick has no request-sequence / abort guard — out-of-order trace responses desync tracedCell vs traceResult and can clobber a newer trace with a stale one
findings.description: handleCellClick synchronously sets tracedCell = {rowIndex, column} for the just-clicked cell, then fires an async traceCell() request whose .then sets traceResult. There is no AbortSignal, no in-flight request tracking, and no "is this still the latest request" check. If a user clicks cell A then cell B before A resolves, both requests run concurrently; whichever resolves LAST wins setTraceResult. When A resolves after B, the node/edge decorations and trace panel (driven by traceResult) show A's trace while the highlighted cell (driven by tracedCell, App.tsx -> DataPreview line 365 isTraced) shows B — a user-visible inconsistency, and the freshly-requested B trace is silently overwritten by the stale A trace.
findings.evidence: Line 210 setTracedCell({rowIndex,column}) updates immediately; lines 211-220 call traceCell({...}) WITHOUT passing args.signal even though TraceCellArgs supports `signal?: AbortSignal` (api/client.ts:541) and traceCell forwards it to post() (client.ts:550). The .then at 221-228 calls setTraceResult(data.trace) unconditionally on success with no guard that this response corresponds to the most recent click. Two overlapping calls resolve in completion order, not request order, so traceResult can reflect an earlier click than tracedCell. App.tsx:598-599/642-643 wire handleCellClick -> onCellClick and tracedCell straight through with no upstream debounce/guard. DataPreview highlights the cell from tracedCell (line 365) while traceResult separately drives nodesWithStatus/edgesWithTrace decorations and the trace detail panel, so the two can disagree.
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a (bug)

findings.title: Duplicated prune-cache-by-seenIds logic between the node projection cache (inlined) and the edge projection cache helper
findings.description: nodesWithStatus inlines a 'if (cache.size > seenIds.size) { for (const id of cache.keys()) if (!seenIds.has(id)) cache.delete(id) }' block (417-421) that is structurally identical to the standalone pruneEdgeProjectionCache helper (144-149). The two operate on different Map value types (CachedProjection vs CachedEdgeProjection) but the prune algorithm is byte-identical. A single generic helper `pruneCacheBySeenIds<T>(cache: Map<string,T>, seenIds: Set<string>)` could back both, removing the duplicated loop. This is distinct from SIMP-04, which targets the per-mode iterate/seen/prune scaffold inside edgesWithTrace, not the node-cache prune.
findings.evidence: Lines 144-149 define pruneEdgeProjectionCache(cache, seenIds) with the exact `if (cache.size <= seenIds.size) return; for (const id of cache.keys()) if (!seenIds.has(id)) cache.delete(id)` body. Lines 417-421 re-implement the same loop inline against projectionCache. Both gate on the size comparison and delete keys absent from seenIds. Behaviour is identical because the algorithm is the same; only the Map's value generic differs, which a generic helper parameterises.
findings.est_reduction: ~5 LOC plus one fewer copy of the prune idiom; net small
findings.behavior_preservation: Generic helper deletes exactly the same keys (those in cache but not seenIds) under the same size guard, so cache contents, reference identities of retained projections, and array outputs are unchanged.

findings.title: emitTablesSig uses '|' delimiter that collides for labels containing '|', so handle re-measure can be skipped on a multi-port retopology
findings.description: `emitTablesSig = emitTableLabels.join("|")` is the value-equality proxy that drives the `useEffect` calling `updateNodeInternals(id)` (lines 241-243) whenever the emit-port set changes. Port labels are RAW table labels and may legally contain the pipe character: the backend (`validate_v2_schema` in src/haute/_api_input_schema.py) only rejects blank/duplicate/sanitised-collision labels, and sanitisation (`_FILESYSTEM_SAFE_RE`) is applied to the parquet *filename* only, never to the label/handle id. Therefore two genuinely different label arrays can produce an identical signature — e.g. `["a", "b|c"]` and `["a|b", "c"]` both join to `"a|b|c"`. When a config commit transitions between two such topologies (handle ids change from `a`,`b|c` to `a|b`,`c`), the effect's deps do not change, `updateNodeInternals(id)` is NOT fired, and React Flow does not re-measure the relabelled right-edge handles, so already-connected edges keep routing to stale handle anchors until an unrelated re-measure occurs. This is exactly the delimiter-collision hazard that the sibling helper `shallowNodeHash.ts` (line 96, `parts.join("")`) deliberately avoids by using a non-printable delimiter; PipelineNode regresses that established convention.
findings.evidence: Line 226-229: emitTableLabels memo = apiInputEmitPortLabels(config) (returns raw labels, only deduped). Line 236: emitTablesSig = emitTableLabels.join("|"). Lines 241-243: useEffect(() => updateNodeInternals(id), [id, emitTablesSig, edgeJoinJoinHandlePosition, updateNodeInternals]). apiInputPorts.ts isPortableLabel only checks trim().length>0 — '|' is permitted. Contrast shallowNodeHash.ts:96 which uses '' precisely to avoid adjacent-value collisions.

findings.title: apiInputEmitPortLabels(config) is computed twice per render for apiInput nodes (once memoized, once inside _SourceHandles)
findings.description: For an apiInput node the port label list is derived twice on every render: once in the `emitTableLabels` useMemo (line 226-229, used for the effect signature and the body label column) and again inside `_SourceHandles` via `apiInputEmitPortLabels(config)` (line 118, used to render the handles). The two call sites are documented as a shared source of truth, but they recompute the same value from the same `nodeData.config` rather than the render passing the already-memoized `emitTableLabels` down to `_SourceHandles`. Threading the memoized array (or its emptiness) into `_SourceHandles` for the apiInput branch would remove the redundant second derivation while keeping the single-source-of-truth guarantee. Pure presentational change; identical handles/labels render. Marginal (the computation is O(tables) and cheap), hence low confidence that it is worth changing.
findings.evidence: Line 118 (_SourceHandles): const labels = apiInputEmitPortLabels(config). Line 226-229 (component body): const emitTableLabels = useMemo(() => isDeployInput ? apiInputEmitPortLabels(nodeData.config) : [], ...). Both consume the same config; _SourceHandles is invoked with the same config object (line 248).
findings.est_reduction: ~3 lines / one redundant O(tables) pass per apiInput render

findings.title: Pattern grouping keeps only the first column's dtype; siblings with a different dtype are misrepresented by the row's dtype badge
findings.description: buildGroups collapses columns that share a numeric-segment pattern (e.g. arr.0, arr.1 -> arr.*) into one PatternRow and records a single dtype. The dtype is captured once on first insertion into patternMap and never reconciled against later columns sharing the same pattern. When sibling columns under the same pattern have heterogeneous dtypes (entirely possible for struct/array-derived flattened columns, e.g. arr.0=Int64, arr.1=Float64), the collapsed row shows only the FIRST concrete column's dtype, silently hiding that the group mixes types.
findings.evidence: Lines 60-62: `if (!patternMap.has(pat)) patternMap.set(pat, { cols: [], dtype: col.dtype }); patternMap.get(pat)!.cols.push(col.name)`. The dtype is written only inside the `!patternMap.has(pat)` branch; subsequent same-pattern columns only `cols.push(col.name)`, never updating dtype. PatternRow.dtype (line 70) therefore equals concreteColumns[0]'s dtype regardless of siblings. It is rendered as the row badge at lines 503-507 via getDtypeColor(row.dtype). Columns arrive from the backend as arbitrary {name,dtype} pairs (types/node.ts ColumnInfo; usePipelineAPI.ts:123-124 sets _columns/_availableColumns verbatim from the API), with no same-pattern dtype-uniformity guarantee.

findings.title: Strip-prefix can author a column_renames entry whose target collides with an existing column, producing a runtime Polars duplicate-name error with no UI guard
findings.description: Stripping a group prefix (or a mid segment) writes column_renames[old] = stripped without checking that `stripped` does not collide with another existing (non-renamed) column. The backend (_execute_lazy._apply_column_renames) builds `valid = {old:new for ... if old in all_cols and old != new}` then calls `frame.rename(valid)`; if two columns end up mapped to the same target, or a rename target equals an untouched existing column name, Polars raises a DuplicateError when the node runs. Because stripGroupPrefix only iterates the rows of one ColumnGroup, it cannot see a same-named column living in a different top-level group, so cross-group collisions are entirely unguarded. The UI lets the user author this invalid config and surfaces the failure only at execution time.
findings.evidence: stripGroupPrefix (191-198) sets `newRenames[col] = stripSegments(col,1)` for each column with no collision check. Concrete collision: columns `licence.type` (top prefix `licence`) and a separate top-level column `type` (top prefix `type`) live in two different ColumnGroups; clicking 'strip licence prefix' yields rename `licence.type -> type`, colliding with the existing `type`. Backend src/haute/_execute_lazy.py:470-472 then does `frame.rename({'licence.type':'type'})` while `type` is already present -> Polars duplicate-column error. No frontend code path validates rename targets against the full column universe (allNames at line 185 is available but unused for this check).

findings.title: Restoring a stripped mid-segment is unreachable when the segment after the group prefix equals the group-prefix name (display says 'stripped' but clicking re-strips)
findings.description: SegmentedName decides whether a segment is stripped by removing the group prefix from the rename value (renamedShort = renamed without leading `groupPrefix.`) and comparing against the pattern, whereas toggleSegmentStrip decides strip-vs-restore from the rename value VERBATIM (currentAfterGroup = newRenames[col] as-is). When the reconstructed rename still begins with the group-prefix segment, these two disagree: the UI strikes the segment through (stripped) but the toggle still finds the target segment present and strips it again (a no-op), so the user can never restore it.
findings.evidence: For group prefix `a` and column `a.a.b` (shortPattern `a.b`), stripping index 0 ('a') reconstructs newFull = groupPrefix + '.' + newAfter = `a.b` (line 251), stored as newRenames['a.a.b']='a.b'. SegmentedName (117-119) computes renamedShort = `a.b`.slice(2) = `b`, parts=['b'], len 1<2 -> marks segment 0 stripped (struck through, line 144-153). On the restore click, toggleSegmentStrip (231-233) sets currentAfterGroup = newRenames['a.a.b'] = `a.b` (verbatim, NOT re-sliced), afterSegments=['a','b']; targetSeg = shortPattern[0]='a'; indexOf('a')=0 and 0<length-1 -> takes the STRIP branch (246-256) again, recomputes newFull='a.b' (unchanged) -> no restore. Restore branch (257-267) is never reached for this column. (For non-coincident names like `g.b.c.d` the verbatim value `g.c.d` no longer contains 'b', so restore works -- confirming the defect is specific to the group-name/segment coincidence.)

findings.title: Loop-invariant, duplicated locals (exampleOriginal / originalFull / groupPrefix) recomputed every iteration inside toggleSegmentStrip
findings.description: Inside `for (const col of row.concreteColumns)`, the code recomputes exampleOriginal = row.concreteColumns[0], originalFull = exampleOriginal (an exact alias), and groupPrefix = topPrefix(originalFull) on every iteration. None depends on the loop variable `col`; all concrete columns of a PatternRow share the same top prefix by construction (they map to one pattern with one topPrefix). exampleOriginal and originalFull are identical, and the whole block is loop-invariant, so it should be hoisted above the loop and the redundant alias removed.
findings.evidence: Lines 226-228: `const exampleOriginal = row.concreteColumns[0]; const originalFull = exampleOriginal; const groupPrefix = topPrefix(originalFull)`. exampleOriginal is referenced nowhere except to initialise originalFull; originalFull is used only to compute groupPrefix. groupPrefix is then used at 233, 250, 251, 260, 261 -- but its value is constant across iterations because buildGroups (66-70) groups by topPrefix(pat), so every col in concreteColumns yields the same topPrefix.
findings.est_reduction: ~2 lines plus per-iteration recomputation
findings.behavior_preservation: Pure refactor: hoist `const groupPrefix = topPrefix(row.concreteColumns[0])` above the loop and delete the exampleOriginal/originalFull aliases; identical values are produced for every iteration, so all downstream branches behave identically.

findings.title: Redundant column-completion reconfigure dispatched on every mount
findings.description: The mount effect (line 343) already configures the column-completion compartment when the EditorView is created (lines 381-385), reading the same `availableColumns` prop. Because effects run in declaration order, the mount effect runs before the `[availableColumns]` effect (line 474). On mount, `viewRef.current` is already set, so the `[availableColumns]` effect immediately dispatches a `columnCompartment.reconfigure(...)` that produces a functionally identical compartment value (a fresh `autocompletion(...)` instance built from the very same prop). This is one extra no-op reconfigure transaction on every component mount. It could be avoided by gating the effect to skip the first run (e.g. an `didMount` ref) or by reconfiguring only when the column set actually differs from what the mount already installed.
findings.evidence: Mount effect lines 381-385 build `columnCompartment.current.of(availableColumns?.length ? autocompletion({override:[columnCompletionSource(availableColumns)]}) : autocompletion())`. Effect at 474-483 then runs on mount (viewRef set) and dispatches `effects: columnCompartment.current.reconfigure(<identical expression>)`. Same `availableColumns` reference in the same render => identical intended config, yet a new extension instance forces CM to apply the reconfigure.
findings.est_reduction: ~1 no-op transaction per mount; ~3 lines if a first-run guard is added
findings.behavior_preservation: Behavior-preserving: the compartment ends in the same configured state; only the extra mount-time reconfigure transaction is eliminated.

findings.title: useRef initializers (Annotation.define / new Compartment) re-evaluated on every render
findings.description: `useRef(Annotation.define<boolean>())` (251), `useRef(new Compartment())` (259) and `useRef(new Compartment())` (260) evaluate their argument on every render even though React keeps only the first result. Each render therefore allocates a throwaway Annotation type and two throwaway Compartment objects that are immediately discarded. The allocations are cheap so the runtime cost is negligible, but it is the well-known `useRef(eagerInit())` anti-pattern; the idiomatic lazy form is `useRef<T>()` populated on first use, or `useState(() => ...)[0]` / a `useMemo` with a stable init so the constructor runs once.
findings.evidence: Line 251 `const externalSyncAnnotation = useRef(Annotation.define<boolean>())`; lines 259-260 `useRef(new Compartment())`. The expression inside useRef(...) is a function-call argument, so JS evaluates it on each render before useRef ignores it past the first.
findings.est_reduction: 3 discarded allocations per render eliminated (no LOC change required if switched to a lazy-init helper)
findings.behavior_preservation: Behavior-preserving: the retained ref values are identical; only the per-render throwaway allocations are removed.

findings.title: Removing a factor leaves orphaned interaction references that flip backend include_main semantics
findings.description: removeFactor() deletes a column only from `terms`, never from `interactions`. Any interaction row that referenced the removed factor is left dangling. This is not merely cosmetic: the dropdown's `value={interaction.factors[n]}` now points to a value absent from the option list (the select renders an inconsistent/blank selection while config still holds the stale factor name), AND the stale name is persisted and sent to the backend.
findings.evidence: removeFactor (l.135) does `const { [name]: _removed, ...rest } = terms; onUpdate("terms", rest)` — interactions untouched. includedFeatures (l.196) is derived only from addedFactors, so the removed name disappears from both dropdowns (l.420, l.430) while interaction.factors still contains it. Backend _build_interactions (src/haute/modelling/_rustystats.py:82-95): a factor not in `terms` takes the fallback `{"type": "categorical"}` (l.86-87) and forces `all_in_terms=False`, so `include_main` is read from config (l.95) and can be True — the exact path the same function's docstring (l.69-74) warns causes main-effect duplication / singular-matrix failure. So removing a factor can silently re-introduce an unconfigured categorical main effect and/or break training with a singular matrix.

findings.title: Interaction dropdowns permit and persist a degenerate self-interaction (same factor on both sides)
findings.description: Dropdown 1 (l.413-421) lists ALL includedFeatures with no filter, while dropdown 2 (l.423-433) filters out only `factors[0]`. If the user picks factor A in dropdown 2 first (factors[1]=A) and then picks A in dropdown 1 (factors[0]=A), the config becomes `factors: ["A","A"]`. Nothing rejects or repairs this. Dropdown 2 then renders `value="A"` against an option list that no longer contains A, so the displayed selection is inconsistent with stored state.
findings.evidence: l.420 renders every `includedFeatures.map(...)` for select-1 (no exclusion of factors[1]). l.430 select-2 does `includedFeatures.filter(f => f !== interaction.factors[0])`. updateInteractionFactor (l.185-193) writes the chosen value unconditionally with no equality guard. Resulting `["A","A"]` reaches backend _build_interactions (src/haute/modelling/_rustystats.py:77-97): len(factors)<2 is False so it is NOT skipped, and the per-factor loop builds a dict keyed by name (l.82-84) which collapses the duplicate to a single key `{"A": {...}, "include_main": False}` — a malformed one-term 'interaction'.

findings.title: Row virtualization start index lacks the upper clamp that column virtualization has, so a stale scrollTop can blank the table after switching to a shorter preview
findings.description: The vertical (row) virtualization computes startIdx with only a lower bound: startIdx = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / ROW_HEIGHT) - OVERSCAN), and endIdx = Math.min(totalRows, ...). There is no upper clamp keeping a full window of rows visible (no equivalent of getColumnWindow's `maxStartIdx = Math.max(0, columnCount - windowSize)` / `startIdx = Math.min(maxStartIdx, ...)`). The scroll div is a persistent, non-keyed element (setScrollContainer is a stable callback ref; the component is not remounted when data.nodeId changes), so scrollTop state survives a data swap. When the user has scrolled a tall preview down (large scrollTop) and the selected node / preview then changes to one with far fewer rows, on the first render with the new data scrollTop still holds the stale large value while totalRows is small. Then startIdx can exceed endIdx, so data.preview.slice(startIdx, endIdx) is empty, topPad = startIdx*ROW_HEIGHT is large, and bottomPad = (totalRows-endIdx)*ROW_HEIGHT = 0 — the body renders only a giant empty top spacer with no data rows. The browser clamps the DOM scrollTop on content shrink and fires a scroll event that eventually corrects the React state, so the blank state is transient (up to one paint), but it is a real flicker and the authors explicitly hardened the analogous column path against exactly this scrolled-then-shrunk scenario (see the dedicated test 'clamps the visible column window when a scrolled preview changes to fewer columns'), making the missing row-side clamp an inconsistency.
findings.evidence: Lines 297-300: `if (shouldVirtualize) { startIdx = Math.max(0, Math.floor(scrollTop / ROW_HEIGHT) - OVERSCAN); endIdx = Math.min(totalRows, Math.ceil((scrollTop + effectiveViewHeight) / ROW_HEIGHT) + OVERSCAN) }`. Compare getColumnWindow (lines 116-119) which clamps: `const maxStartIdx = Math.max(0, columnCount - windowSize); const startIdx = Math.min(maxStartIdx, Math.max(0, rawStart - COLUMN_OVERSCAN))`. With e.g. previous scrollTop=10000 (≈357 rows down) and new totalRows=5: startIdx = max(0, 357-10)=347, endIdx = min(5, ...)=5, slice(347,5)=[] -> blank body, topPad=347*28.
findings.behavior_preservation: n/a

findings.title: Invalid coordinate-less touch drop throws instead of being ignored (point computed before isValid guard)
findings.description: In the source-to-source branch of onConnectEnd, connectionEndPoint(event) is evaluated on line 247 BEFORE the `if (connectionState.isValid === false) return` guard on line 248. connectionEndPoint throws 'Connection end touch event did not include pointer coordinates' when a TouchEvent has empty touches and changedTouches. Therefore an INVALID connection (isValid === false) that happens to be a coordinate-less touch end will throw an uncaught error inside the React event handler, instead of being silently discarded as an invalid gesture should be. Hoisting the `isValid === false` early-return above the connectionEndPoint(event) call fixes this and is behaviour-preserving for every currently-tested path.
findings.evidence: Lines 242-248: branch entered when fromHandle.type==='source' && toHandle.type==='source' && targetNodeId. Line 247 `const point = screenToFlowPosition(connectionEndPoint(event))` runs first; connectionEndPoint (lines 61-68) throws when both event.touches[0] and event.changedTouches[0] are undefined. Line 248 `if (connectionState.isValid === false) return` only runs after. The existing throw test (test line 1261) uses isValid:true; the invalid-drop test (test line 392) uses a MouseEvent with coordinates, so the isValid:false + coordinate-less-touch combination is uncovered and would crash.

findings.title: Transient UI key `_id` is persisted into the saved banding config and sent over the wire
findings.description: `ensureRuleIds` injects a frontend-only `_id` field into each rule object, and the id-assignment effect persists it back via `onUpdateFactor({ rules })`. This patch flows through BandingEditor.updateFactor -> onUpdate('factors', next) into the saved pipeline config. `normaliseBandingFactors` (bandingUtils.ts:3-7) returns the persisted factors array verbatim and never strips `_id`, and the backend rule reader (_banding_config.py uses plain dict.get, no extra='forbid') simply ignores the unknown key. Net effect: a purely-presentational React key (only needed for <tr key=...>) leaks into the persisted domain model and the request payload. It does not crash anything, but it pollutes saved configs with non-deterministic values (`rule_<seq>_<Date.now base36>`), which also defeats config diffing/equality and round-trips junk to disk/server. The id is a render concern and should be derived/held outside the persisted `rules` (e.g. a WeakMap keyed by rule object, or a ref-held parallel id list), not merged into the wire object.
findings.evidence: Line 27: `return { ...r, _id: nextRuleId() }`. Line 214: `onUpdateFactor({ rules })` persists ids. bandingUtils.ts:5 `if (Array.isArray(raw) && raw.length > 0) return raw` — no _id stripping. _banding_config.py:70 `result['rules'] = normalise_banding_rules(...)` keeps original rule dicts (including _id) when no categorical expansion happens.

findings.title: Stable-id assignment uses two refs plus a dependency-less effect performing a render-phase state write-back
findings.description: Stable row keys are produced by: (a) calling `ensureRuleIds(rawRules)` on every render, (b) a `prevRulesRef`/`didAssignIds` ref pair plus a `[rawRules]` effect to reset a guard, and (c) a second effect with intentionally no deps that runs after every render to fire `onUpdateFactor({ rules })`. This is a side-effecting write-back of persisted state purely to obtain React keys, and its correctness depends on the parent round-tripping `_id` unchanged and not memo-stripping it. The whole mechanism can be replaced by deriving keys without persisting them — e.g. a module-level `WeakMap<rule, string>` assigned lazily inside `ruleKey`, or `useMemo` mapping rule identity to ids — which removes both refs, both effects, the eslint-disable on the no-dep effect, and the parent write-back entirely. That also resolves finding #1 (no `_id` ever enters the wire model).
findings.evidence: Lines 201-216: `didAssignIds`/`prevRulesRef` + `useEffect(...,[rawRules])` reset + `useEffect(() => { if (rules !== rawRules && !didAssignIds.current) { ...; onUpdateFactor({ rules }) } })` with comment '// intentionally no deps — runs on every render'. `ruleKey` (line 33-35) already falls back to `fallback_${index}` so keys never hard-depend on persisted `_id`.
findings.est_reduction: ~15-20 lines (remove ensureRuleIds persistence, two refs, two effects, one eslint-disable)
findings.behavior_preservation: Row keys remain stable across edits/reorders via object-identity map; deletion/insert behavior and all existing tests on _id presence would need updating since _id would no longer be emitted to onUpdateFactor (behavioral change limited to the synthetic key, not rule data).

findings.title: onPaste handlers on the operator <select> elements never fire (paste is not dispatched on <select>)
findings.description: The lower/upper operator cells render `<select ... onPaste={(e) => handleCellPaste(e, i, 0|2)}>`. The whole-grid container paste (`handlePaste`) still covers operator data because it parses full rows, so functionality is not lost — the cell-level handlers on selects are simply unreachable code carrying the `fieldIndex` 0/2 mapping for op columns.

Compare TwoWayGrid.tsx where onPaste is only attached to <input> cells (lines 250, 321), not selects.

findings.title: hasSelectedColumn uses strict `selected === true`, diverging from the backend's truthiness check on malformed/legacy configs
findings.description: `hasSelectedColumn` decides whether a table contributes a port by testing `(c).selected === true` (strict). The backend predicate this module explicitly claims to mirror — `_json_shred.table_is_emitting` — instead uses Python truthiness: `any(isinstance(col, dict) and col.get("selected") for col in columns)`. For the common, editor-produced configs the two agree (the editor's `writeV2` always persists `selected` as a strict boolean, and a missing/`false` key is falsy on both sides). They diverge only for a column whose `selected` is truthy-but-not-`true` (e.g. `selected: 1`, `selected: "y"`, `selected: {}`): the backend counts such a table as emitting (renders/binds a port at runtime), while `hasSelectedColumn` returns false, so `apiInputEmitPortLabels` omits the port and `_SourceHandles` won't render it. Because the same function gates BOTH frontend rendering and the backend's runtime port set, a desync here is precisely the silent-orphan / missing-port class the module's header says it exists to prevent. The config reaches this code unnormalised: `nodeData.config` is stored opaquely and only coerced lazily by `readV2` when the editor opens, so a hand-authored or legacy on-disk config with a non-boolean `selected` flows straight into `hasSelectedColumn`.
findings.evidence: apiInputPorts.ts:46 `(c as { selected?: unknown }).selected === true` vs _json_shred.py:176 `return any(isinstance(col, dict) and col.get("selected") for col in columns)`. Reachability: App stores config verbatim; readV2 (apiInputSchema.ts:120) only normalises when the editor is open. Note readV2 itself treats missing `selected` as selected (`cc.selected !== false`), a third interpretation, underscoring that `selected` truthiness is handled inconsistently across the three sites.

findings.title: Zustand stores subscribed without selectors, re-rendering the host (App) on every unrelated UI/toast change
findings.description: The hook destructures `const { setSyncBanner } = useUIStore()` and `const { addToast } = useToastStore()` with no selector argument. Calling a Zustand store hook with no selector subscribes the consuming component to the ENTIRE store object, so it re-renders on ANY state change in that store. useUIStore holds high-churn UI state (hoveredNodeId, paletteOpen/utilityOpen/importsOpen/gitOpen toggles, nodePanelWidth, per-node editor section maps, nodeSearchOpen, syncBanner). useWebSocketSync is mounted directly in App.tsx (App.tsx:278), so App and its whole subtree re-render on every hover-highlight change, panel toggle, and toast push, even though this hook only ever needs the two stable action functions. The project's own selector contract is documented verbatim in useGraphStore.ts ("Consumers MUST subscribe via selectors so unrelated state changes do not trigger re-renders ... `useGraphStore()` // BAD — re-renders on any change"); these two lines violate it. The fix is `useUIStore((s) => s.setSyncBanner)` and `useToastStore((s) => s.addToast)`.
findings.evidence: Trace: useUIStore (stores/useUIStore.ts) is `create<UIState>()((set) => ({...}))` with many fields incl. hoveredNodeId/setHoveredNodeId (108-109) updated on hover. `const { setSyncBanner } = useUIStore()` (line 93) reads the whole store → component subscribes to all of it → any `set(...)` (e.g. setHoveredNodeId) triggers a re-render of the hook's host. App.tsx:278 calls `useWebSocketSync({...})` at the top level of App, so App re-renders. The actions themselves (setSyncBanner at useUIStore.ts:87, addToast in useToastStore) are stable refs defined once in `create`, so the effect dep array [..., setSyncBanner, addToast] does NOT change and the WebSocket is NOT torn down — confirming this is a render-cost/contract issue, not a reconnect bug. The remedy (selector subscription) is exactly the pattern useGraphStore.ts documents and that other call sites follow.
findings.est_reduction: ~0 LOC (change 2 lines to selector form); eliminates App-subtree re-renders on every UI-store and toast-store mutation
findings.behavior_preservation: Behavior-preserving: selectors return the identical stable action references the hook already uses; only the over-broad subscription (and resulting redundant re-renders) is removed. No change to WebSocket lifecycle, message handling, or any user-visible behavior.

findings.title: FileBrowser cache-hit path does not clear a stale error, leaving a successfully-loaded directory hidden behind a stale error banner
findings.description: In the FileBrowser effect, the cache-hit fast path (`if (cached) { setItems(...); setLoading(false); return }`) returns without calling `setError(null)`. Only the cache-miss branch resets the error (line 189). Because the render checks `error` BEFORE `items` (lines 250-251), a stale error from a previously-failed directory persists and masks the cached content of a different, successfully-loaded directory.
findings.evidence: Reachable sequence: (1) User is in directory B which loads OK and is cached (setFileListCache, line 195; cache TTL 30s per useSettingsStore.getFileListCache). (2) User navigates into subdir A; A's listFiles rejects -> catch sets error + items=[] (lines 200-201); note A is NOT cached on failure. (3) User clicks goUp back to B; goUp sets loading(true) then setDir(B) (lines 211-212). (4) Effect re-runs for B, getFileListCache(B) hits -> setItems(B), setLoading(false), `return` at line 187 WITHOUT setError(null). Render at lines 250-251 evaluates `error ? <error> : items...`, so B's valid cached rows are hidden behind A's stale error banner until the 30s cache expires or `extensions` changes. The cache-miss branch clears error (line 189) but the cache-hit branch does not.

findings.title: InputSourcesBar uses non-unique varName as React key, causing key collisions and mis-targeted delete buttons when two upstream sources share a sanitized name
findings.description: InputSourcesBar renders `inputSources.map((src) => <span key={src.varName} ...>)`. `varName` is NOT unique: in NodePanel.tsx (line 636) it is computed as `sanitizeName(nodeMap[e.source]?.data.label || e.source)`, derived from the upstream node label. sanitizeName is many-to-one, so distinct upstream nodes whose labels collapse to the same identifier produce identical `varName` values and therefore duplicate React keys. The struct already carries a guaranteed-unique `edgeId` (e.g. used as the delete payload `onDeleteInput(src.edgeId)`), which is the correct key.
findings.evidence: Producer (NodePanel.tsx lines 632-639): `upstreamEdges.map((e) => ({ sourceNodeId: e.source, varName: sanitizeName(nodeMap[e.source]?.data.label || e.source), sourceLabel: ..., edgeId: e.id }))`. sanitizeName (utils/sanitizeName.ts:18-19) replaces `[\s-]` with `_` and strips non-alnum/underscore, so labels like `"Age Band"`, `"Age-Band"`, `"Age_Band"`, and `"Age Band!"` all sanitize to `"Age_Band"`. Two upstream nodes with such labels yield two inputSources entries with identical `varName` -> `key={src.varName}` collides. React then logs a duplicate-key warning and, on reconciliation, can associate the click handler / DOM of the wrong entry; clicking one delete-X may remove the other source's edge (both call onDeleteInput but the reconciled element identity is ambiguous). Fix: `key={src.edgeId}` (edgeId = e.id, unique per edge).
